title: Going global: don't wait until you're big to go to Europe and America — go there first to get big
dek: Wei Zhe says many companies think they'll go to Europe and America once they're big, but it's exactly the reverse — you go there to become big. Get the region choice wrong and the later product 3.0 and channel pyramid won't stand up.
why: Wei Zhe compresses ten years of overseas investment experience into four choices, counterintuitive but each backed by cases and numbers, especially the second half on AI transforming organizations and pricing, which is the most information-dense.
who: Founders building or preparing to build overseas brands, cross-border e-commerce operators, and early-stage investors watching consumer going global.
skip: The opening small talk and 15th anniversary congratulations, about 1 minute, can be skipped.

points.h: The old cross-border mega-seller path is dead
points.body: Wei Zhe says the ‘cross-border mega-seller’ popular in Shenzhen is a distribution-style mindset, with dozens or hundreds of accounts; he has seen companies with over a thousand accounts and hundreds of thousands of SKUs. A decade ago these companies made money faster than other paths, and many investors loved them. But distribution-style companies are essentially traffic-style companies: the more stores, the more likely to get traffic. When platforms don't have enough goods, distribution isn't opposed; once goods are abundant, using distribution to grab traffic is bad money driving out good. More critically, three red lines: selling goods not as described harms consumers, fake orders harm other merchants, and inserting small cards to build private domains harms the platform. Amazon's flywheel places great importance on consumer experience, and these behaviors hit exactly that protective wall.

Wei Zhe says it's not just cross-border e-commerce; all of life is about choices being more important than effort. He gives four choices: region, channel, product category, and brand positioning. On region, he has always advocated seizing the European and American markets first, because of strong purchasing power, high internet penetration, and more importantly, the brand can build momentum. This isn't their invention; when Japanese and Korean brands went global, they all seized Europe and America. On category, they change their advice every three years: the first three years they supported products with universal appeal between China and abroad, where the domestic supply chain could sell overseas without modification, like Anker's power banks, which were almost identical except for voltage; the second three years they advised making overseas-exclusive products, because China's supply chain had gone global and universal products had no differentiation; the most recent three years is product 3.0 — electric, with chips, with algorithms.

points.h: It's not that you go to Europe and America after getting big; you get big by going there
points.body: Many companies tell Wei Zhe, ‘I'll go to Europe and America when I'm big,’ and he says it's exactly the reverse: you go to Europe and America to become big. He gives the example of Cupshe, a swimwear company: a husband and wife, with $50,000 of inventory, and their first stop was the US. $50,000 is the goods for sale, actually very little, so there's no minimum threshold. He recently looked at AI smart hardware, starting from Kickstarter crowdfunding with a thousand or ten thousand products, even taking pre-orders before placing orders, with no capital — that's also a great way to test the waters. He even advises big companies entering the European and American markets to learn from small startups. They always say the needle must be fine enough to pierce; both big and small companies should first do the four singles well: single market, single category, single channel, single brand.

points.h: After AI, good companies don't just find demand, they create it
points.body: Wei Zhe says with AI, excellent companies don't look for demand, they should lead demand and create demand. He gives the example of a Chinese company making astronomical telescopes: originally not electric, they electrified it, added chips and algorithms; the algorithm is actually simple, with GPS positioning, and the map of the universe's movements is regular. He wasn't an astronomy enthusiast but would buy one; at home in Silicon Valley, with one tap, it automatically aligns to Orion for you, tells you the best viewing is at 3 a.m., you set it and go to sleep, and the next day it takes the photos for you. This lets everyone become a good astronomy enthusiast. Another example: a cross-border class student making curtains, which didn't sell well in the US after being electrified because American electricians are expensive, so he put solar panels on the window, turning electric curtains that need an electrician into DIY ones; revenue went from one or two hundred million to four or five hundred million, with profit of one or two hundred million.

points.h: In the AI era, still using subscription fees means you're behind
points.body: Wei Zhe says in the AI era, if you still think in terms of subscription fees, you're behind again; they are all advising companies to do back-end charging, software charging, called tokenized. A monthly subscription fee is the dumbest way, a bit like advertising charging by time instead of by usage. This time AI has brought out the most ideal charging model in all of human education: paying according to your usage of AI software, services, or content. He gives an example: Bessie, if you take two weeks off this month, isn't subscribing for a month a waste of two weeks? They suggest that AI-transformed hardware should be charged like AI, not the old SaaS model of $9.9 per month. An AI reading platform he looked at charges by how many articles you read, and nothing if you don't read; the same with smart bike trainers: after topping up, one dollar per ride, two dollars for two hours.

points.h: Adding AI is more promising than AI plus
points.body: Wei Zhe has a view called AI plus or plus AI; he reverses the phrase and says he's more optimistic about plus AI rather than today's AI plus. The difference: plus AI is taking hardware humans have already accepted and making it AI; rather than creating a previously unseen hardware because of AI. It's very hard for humans to accept a brand-new hardware. For example, Oura makes rings, because you first accepted rings; some things that hang a camera under your neck are harder for me, I haven't accepted that hardware. So they are very optimistic about adding AI to already-accepted hardware. They invested in a capacitive stylus that is number one globally, because everyone already writes on a Pad, it doesn't add an extra pen, it just makes your pen AI. He also especially wants to transform one of the top fitness equipment companies going global, replacing the fitness coach on the screen with AI-generated ones — you want a male, it's male; you want a Black person, it's Black; install two cameras and you get AI-guided fitness.

points.h: Channels aren't flat; they're a pyramid
points.body: Wei Zhe says channels aren't multiple channels multiple paths, each channel parallel or even competing; excellent brands all have a channel pyramid. Like luxury brands and traditional brands, there must be different channel strategies, pricing strategies, and which channel new products launch in first. What is a light-goods channel, what is the main waist volume channel — the pyramid design differs by category and brand. He gives Anker: making power bank mecha seems a bit low, to enter the consumer electronics high ground of Soundcore earphones you have to get into Apple flagship stores; whether it really sells a lot isn't important, but it can transform the brand, Apple is the pyramid's peak. Pop Mart must open on London's Oxford Street, even if it doesn't make money, how much can it lose, but it must be propped up there. He says some companies treat Temu and AliExpress as parallel channels to sell goods, which definitely won't work; AliExpress is a light-goods channel, when Amazon delists you, you dump it there, you can't sell on Amazon and here too, consumers get confused.

Wei Zhe says he really dislikes spending heavily on marketing. Many Chinese brands going global or cross-border e-commerce are willing to add 2% of revenue to marketing expenses, but consumers don't get it. He says, do you dare to add 2% of revenue to R&D expenses? He has met many bosses with 1 billion or 2 billion scale; a 1 billion boss says 20 million for R&D, I don't know what for. He says, see, there's the problem, you don't know what for. Your 2% on marketing makes the platform happy, consumers don't get it; but 2% into R&D, consumers get it. He has always firmly believed good products speak for themselves, marketing is just — your R&D is 1, marketing is 0; if you have something good you can amplify it, if you don't have that 1, never put many 0s. He gives three judgment signals: first, dare to find a benchmark company, definitely a mid-to-upper brand, and you crush it by doubling performance; second, you sell at the same high price as it; third, you sell online and hit offline channels to come to you.

points.h: AI doesn't just change products, it transforms every position
points.body: Wei Zhe says AI has two important things for companies, big, medium, and small all need to do well: first, the combination of products with AI; second, how the organization changes through AI. He sees cross-border e-commerce companies as almost the industry most in need of using AI to transform every position among all he has seen. Every position should ask what AI can do for you: product selection, content generation, ad placement choices — essentially all algorithms; previously relying on human experience, and experience is definitely not as powerful as algorithmic iteration. Customer service AI-ified, no more customer service, customer service is just you training your customer service agent; ad placement you train an agent; product selection, product display, product image and video generation all AI-ified. He says this is the first and only industry he has seen where the entire company's organizational chain can be transformed by AI. He also says they most oppose placing many people overseas, with or without AI, called no unnecessary overseas staffing.

points.h: Don't just let AI do the work, let it make decisions
points.body: Wei Zhe explains AI and organization very simply: many companies have P series and M series, P is professional, M is management. Many people are used to letting AI do P work, doing the work; generating images was originally a P series job. But truly great companies don't just let AI do P series work, they gradually let it do the work of Manager, Director, VP. He gives a real case of AI pricing: the company originally wanted to sell at 35 euros, AI said you can sell at 55, the company really went to 55, and it really sold, volume similar to before at 35, but earning 20 euros more. He says AI has no courage, it's bolder than you, it has compared everything across the web. He also says even if AI hallucinates, with so many large models in China and the US, they won't dream the same dream at the same time, so you must cross-validate.

terms.def: Wei Zhe's term for a charging model based on AI usage, replacing monthly subscriptions.
Wei Zhe's coined term: daring to define a price and not lowering it; when peers catch up to the same performance, you compete on performance.
Single market, single category, single channel, single brand — Wei Zhe advises overseas companies to focus first.
Wei Zhe's overseas category advice: from non-electric to electric, electric with chips, chips with AI algorithms.

facts.v: from one or two hundred million to four or five hundred million

quotes.text: Price-performance ratio means my performance and quality are the same, you match me, and I compete on price. Price-performance ratio is what I dare to define; after I set it, I don't lower the price. If a peer catches up to the same performance, I increase performance.
Many companies tell me, I'll go to Europe and America when I'm big. I say it's exactly the reverse: you go to Europe and America to become big.

You say a non-electric product gets copied by others in a month. Electric? You also have many European and American access requirements, you'll probably lead by six months. OK, your chip can add another twelve months. OK, your algorithm might lead for a lifetime.

Independent sites or independent apps: the kung fu is beyond the transaction. They have four major functions. Very few Chinese companies, except those we coach, pay any attention to the other three functions.
